issues.description: trainer_args key mismatch: docstring says max_steps/val_interval but code reads max_step and never uses val_interval
issues.detail: The docstring lists `max_steps`, `log_interval`, `val_interval`, `save_interval`, but __init__ reads `trainer_args["max_step"]` (singular) and `val_interval` is never read at all. Either the config schema is wrong or the code is wrong, but they cannot both be right. Pick one and make the code, docstring, and config agree. This is exactly the kind of drift that bites the next maintainer in six months when val_interval silently does nothing.

issues.description: validation runs every save_interval steps with no separate cadence, and ignores val_interval entirely
issues.detail: run() calls self.train() (which advances save_interval steps), then self.valid() unconditionally, then saves a checkpoint. So validation cadence is wired to save cadence and `val_interval` from the documented config is dead. If save_interval is large, valid is rare; if small, validation thrashes the loop. State what the cadence is supposed to be and implement that. Right now the loop lies about what it does.

issues.description: torch.cuda.set_device(args.local_rank) before validating local_rank is not None
issues.detail: main() does `torch.cuda.set_device(args.local_rank)` immediately. local_rank defaults to None and the help string admits the launcher is supposed to set it. If a user runs the script directly or via a launcher that uses LOCAL_RANK env var instead of the CLI flag, this blows up with a confusing TypeError instead of a useful error. Read from env (LOCAL_RANK) as a fallback and assert it's a non-negative int with a real error message.

issues.description: argparse flag naming is inconsistent: dashes vs underscores
issues.detail: Most flags use dashes (--train-config, --output-dir) but --local_rank and --resume_path use underscores. Pick one. Mixed conventions are exactly the kind of small-but-annoying inconsistency that makes a CLI feel sloppy. argparse rewrites dashes to underscores in the namespace anyway, so just use dashes everywhere.

issues.description: specifier parsing uses split() on whitespace for arbitrarily-formatted strings
issues.detail: `args.valid_unregistered_specifier.split()` assumes specifiers are whitespace-separated, but the help text says format is `task:name:data_json[:factor]` and never says you can have multiple. If a path contains a space (yes, this happens) or you use commas like a normal person, you get silent breakage or a weird parse error inside DataIteratorFactory. Document the separator explicitly and pick something that doesn't collide with shell quoting. Same issue for the registered variant.

issues.description: checkpoint sort by 'step_' substring is fragile
issues.detail: `x.name.split("step_")[-1]` and the filter `"step_" in d.name` will match any directory whose name contains 'step_' anywhere. If someone creates `pre_step_warmup` or `step_final`, this either picks the wrong one or crashes on int(). Use a strict prefix check (`d.name.startswith("step_")`) and parse the trailing integer with a try/except that logs and skips bad names. Cheap to do right.

issues.description: valid() builds all_stats but never resets between datasets and accumulates across batches naively
issues.detail: all_stats is created fresh per dataset (good), but the per-batch values are appended as Python floats and averaged with sum()/len(). That ignores batch size, so unequal final batches skew the mean. Either weight by batch size or use the same reduce-then-divide pattern the train loop uses. Also: the comment '(should be outside the batch loop)' suggests the author already knows there's a bug here. Fix it instead of commenting on it.

The function iterates `for key in stats:` and later assigns `stats[key] = stats[key] / world_size` for each key. Reassigning existing keys during iteration is fine in CPython for plain dicts, but the first loop holds tensor handles in a list and the second loop divides in-place — this works but is brittle. More importantly, if stats contains non-tensor entries today or tomorrow, the assert kills the whole reduce. Either pre-validate, or skip non-tensors with a warning. Right now any contributor adding a scalar to stats blows up training.

issues.description: wandb is a hard dependency and silently mandatory across the codepath
issues.detail: The trainer docstring says wandb is MANDATORY and 'will raise an error if wandb.run is None' — but it doesn't actually check. It just calls wandb.config.update and wandb.log, which will fail with a less-useful error if wandb isn't initialized. Either add the assert the docstring promises, or stop promising it. Forcing wandb on every user is also a strong choice for a research codebase; at minimum document why a no-op logger isn't acceptable.

issues.description: logging suppression for non-rank-0 sets level to CRITICAL — INFO logs from libraries on other ranks are still useful for debugging
issues.detail: Setting log_level='CRITICAL' on all non-zero ranks means when one rank crashes you get nothing from it. At least leave WARNING on, or write per-rank log files. Silence-by-default is fine for stdout, but losing crash context is not.

This PR adds the launcher, the trainer, and the wandb integration policy in one shot. The wandb-is-mandatory decision is a separable design choice and would be easier to review (and revert) on its own. Not a blocker, but next time: three patches.

issues.description: train_dtype belongs as a module-level function or staticmethod
issues.detail: It doesn't use self. Make it a @staticmethod or pull it out. Minor, but the codebase will accumulate these if nobody pushes back.

New trainer, new launcher, no tests. I get that distributed training is hard to unit-test, but _load_checkpoint's sorting logic, _all_reduce_stats' tensor handling, and train_dtype's branching are all pure-Python and testable. Add a few. The maintainer six years from now will thank you.

review.summary: Two new files, ~500 lines, decent shape overall but with real bugs that should block merge. The biggest problems are config-schema drift (docstring says max_steps/val_interval, code reads max_step and never uses val_interval at all) and a validation loop that's wired to save cadence rather than the documented val_interval — these are both lies the code tells about itself, and they will burn the next person who edits this. Smaller issues cluster around CLI hygiene (mixed dash/underscore flags, naive whitespace-split specifier parsing, unguarded local_rank), fragile checkpoint discovery via substring match, and a valid() loop that averages floats without weighting by batch size while the author has helpfully commented that they know it's wrong. NEEDS-WORK: fix the config-schema/cadence lies, harden the CLI and checkpoint parsing, make valid() honest, and either enforce the wandb assertion the docstring promises or drop the promise. Add the obvious pure-Python tests on the way.
